chapter: Later life, World's Fair and Ellington
title: Too intelligent and a troublemaker: speaking up on the bandstand
summary: Hall explains how he is seen as a troublemaker, with a daylight saving anecdote.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: I think we got caught with the tape -- tape stop before. I just wanted to go over something that may or may not be on the last reel. You said you had never -- have stopped trying to get into this field and -- okay, now in the day of your Black newscasters on most of the different channels it has become quite a different story then. Then there was no quota; now there is a quota, but we said now maybe you've been rejected because of age.
Right.
And then I raised the point that -- did you ever get the feeling that sometimes it was because you were too intelligent?
Yes.
And I, you know, counted with that I've felt that at certain times, because they don't want people, anyone who will make waves.
Absolutely.
And you said this goes on on the bandstand as well. And I said, how does it manifest itself on the bandstand?
Right.
That's where we --
Oh, and I was going to give you a for instance, right?

Well, say -- and this has happened several times to me -- say on a Saturday night at the change of time from standard to daylight and you're supposed to finish at 1:00 o'clock -- you're supposed to finish at 2:00 o'clock.
2:00 o'clock, but it becomes.
But it either becomes 1:00 o'clock or 3:00 o'clock.
At 2:00 o'clock.
So I've always had something to say about this extra hour one way or the other, so that right away makes you a troublemaker.
(Laughter.)

I was working at the Blue Angel in one of these instances, and I knew we were going to finish at 2:00 o'clock, and the last train to Port Chester was something like, well, that was available, that I could make it other than waiting about four or five hours for the next train, because I've got a golf date in Port Chester with a friend, and they were going to meet me at the station.
So comes time the end of the job, I'm ready to go. You know, well, where you going? We're finished. Oh, no, time change. You got another hour.
Really?
That's a mild one. There are many more intricate ones than that.
Well, what do you -- I was going to say how does it manifest itself in the interaction amongst the musicians at this --
Well, nobody else is saying anything about it.
Oh, you're always the guy that speaks up.
Yeah. Yeah, like always.
(Laughter.)
Everyone else reaps the benefits.
(Laughter.)
Yeah, well, there's something that certain people can sense, like when you're being interviewed and everything like that, that you're not going to be a person who is a follower. You're a leader type.
Well, I can't be -- I can't be a follower. I hate that.
And yet you've been --

I was a Boy Scout, and -- and everybody traveled in packs. Then when I was working in the theater on matinee days, there were always groups going out to eat together. I couldn't stand that. I watched all of this when I worked at the World's Fair, how people just -- just followed, you know, in the --
Uh-huh. Well, people want to be
part of a group, you know.
Well, I'm not an isolationist,
I know you're not.
You know, I just don't want anyone else to control my movements.
